justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish but relatively stable near-term outlook. For the 1-day estimate around 219.5, I was essentially anchoring to recent price action and assuming mean-reversion dynamics would dominate over a very short horizon, with minimal directional drift. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher to 221, reflecting a modest positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run equity risk premium embedded in broad market ETFs or stocks trading in this range. The 1-month estimate at 224 continues that gentle upward trajectory, compounding the same drift assumption over roughly 22 trading days. In all three cases, the point estimates are driven primarily by the current price level plus a small expected return, without assuming any major catalyst in either direction.

The confidence interval widths are calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. Over one day, price moves are constrained by normal intraday and overnight volatility, so the 90% CI spans roughly 15 points — a relatively tight band. Over one week, uncertainty compounds as daily volatility accumulates, widening the interval to about 30 points. Over one month, the interval expands to roughly 60 points, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty alongside the possibility that macro or fundamental conditions shift meaningfully. I also applied slightly fatter tails than a pure normal distribution would suggest, given that equity markets historically exhibit skewness and kurtosis in their return distributions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected rise in unemployment, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could trigger a sharp selloff exceeding the lower bound of even the 1-month interval. A surprise hawkish pivot from central banks or a liquidity shock could similarly compress valuations quickly. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong earnings season, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical risk could accelerate buying and push prices above the upper bounds. These tail scenarios are real but were assigned low enough probability that they sit outside the 90% CI by design, though they are far from impossible.
